speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (for the Minister of Justice) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-92, an act to amend the Northwest Territories Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-92 is a proposed amendment to the Northwest Territories Act to approve an amendment by the territorial government to its Official Languages Act, to extend the delay for the translation and bilingual printing and publishing of territorial laws.
In 1984 the government of the Northwest Territories reached an agreement with the federal government to make French an official language of territorial legislative and governmental institutions and to provide for government services in French.
The agreement provided that the territorial government would adopt a law on official languages that would be entrenched by federal legislation so that any amendment by the territorial government which would affect

November 23, 1990
Government Orders
rights or services provided therein would require the approval of Parliament.
Under the agreement, the costs of implementing French as an official language have been borne by the federal government. As well, the agreement provided for federal funding of $16 million to the territories for preservation and enhancement of aboriginal languages and services in those languages.
In 1988, Parliament passed the new federal Official Languages Act. The act specifically excluded legislative and governmental institutions of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon from the definition of federal institutions. It also excluded the laws of the territories and the Yukon from the bilingual requirements applying to federal laws.
As contemplated by the 1984 agreement, the act also entrenched in the Northwest Territories Act and the Yukon Act, the respective language ordinances of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
Section 45.1 of the Northwest Territories Act, and its counterpart in the Yukon Act require the approval of Parliament for any amendment to the territorial law, except where it provides for additional rights and services in English and in French or the aboriginal languages.
Since January 19, 1990 all new territorial legislation has been introduced and passed in the Territorial Assembly in both English and French. In April 1990 the territorial government amended its official languages ordinance to make six aboriginal languages the official languages of the territories, along with French and English.
The amendment also provided for a number of additional rights and government services in the aboriginal languages.
The April amendment provides, for instance, that the government may prescribe the translation and publication of ordinances in one or more of the aboriginal languages after their enactment in English and French.
As well, by January 1, 1993 territorial government services will be provided in each of the official aboriginal languages where there is significant demand in those languages.
In August 1990 the Minister of Justice of the Northwest Territories wrote to the federal Minister of Justice to seek agreement on an amendment to the Northwest Territories Act to concur in a territorial amendment to the official languages ordinance to extend the time limit for the translation into French and bilingual printing and publishing of previously enacted laws to March 31, 1992. In the letter and in subsequent meetings, Mr. Ballantyne and his officials explained that the need to extend the delay resulted from technical problems in reprinting the revised ordinances and adjusting the regulations accordingly.
I understand a further factor in meeting the deadline has been the difficulty in attracting and keeping qualified legal translators, who are in very short supply in Canada.
The revised ordinances are in final revision and are being sent to the printers, but they cannot be brought into force until the regulations are also ready. Experts from the translation bureau of the Department of the Secretary of State have verified this. They agree that the delay period requested is an appropriate one, in view of the remaining work to be done.
The Minister of Justice of the Northwest Territories has assured us, and other ministers of the territorial government have confirmed, that the delay in bringing their laws into effect in both English and French will not have any impact on the requirement of the territorial law that services in both languages will be available from the territorial government as of January 1, 1991. That was an important factor in the government's decision to seek concurrence by Parliament.
If the concurring amendment to the Northwest Territories is not made, the amendment to the territorial official languages ordinance would be ineffective in extending the delay. By virtue of the official languages ordinance, the consequence would be that virtually all territorial laws would become of no force or effect as of January 1, 1991.
The operation and enforcement of law would be seriously compromised in the territories. We cannot accept responsibility for such a result.
The government of the territories is well on its way to meeting its obligations under the territorial official languages ordinance. It needs a further period to finish

November 23, 1990

the work it has undertaken in revising its laws and regulations, and printing and publishing them in both official languages.
On October 29, 1990 the territorial legislature and the commissioner in council, passed an act to amend the Official Languages Act to extend the deadline for bilingual printing and publishing of previous legislation until March 31, 1992.
Bill C-92, an act to amend the Northwest Territories Act, would simply demonstrate Parliament's concurrence in that amendment and prevent a potentially serious gap in the operation and the validity of the laws of the Northwest Territories. To avoid such a result, Parliament's concurring, through this amendment, will be required prior to December 31.
I hope all members will recognize the need to act quickly in a non-partisan spirit to meet our responsibilities to the people of the north.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-92, whose purpose is to grant the Northwest Territories an extension of the agreement by which all legislative documents, assembly proceedings and other documents shall be available in both official languages, that is, English and French, by April 1991.
Madam Speaker, we are all familiar with the situation concerning official languages in the Territories, a situation that was described quite satisfactorily by the parliamentary secretary. Section 9 of the Territories' Official Languages Act reads as follows:
[English)
It reads as follows, Madam Speaker: "English and French are the official languages of the Territories and have equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all institutions of the Legislative Assembly and Government of the Territories".
Article 10 of that same Official Languages Act reads as follows: "Everyone has the right to use English or French in any debates or other proceedings of the Legislative Assembly".
What we are dealing with today is an act to amend the Northwest Territories Act and allow for a second exten-
Govemment Orders
sion to the commitments made by the Northwest Territories to translate and make available legislative documents to the people of the Northwest Territories.

Madam Speaker, I would like to provide some historical background. In 1984, the Government of Canada, represented by Liberal Minister Serge Joyal at the time, and the Government of the Northwest Territories signed an agreement under which the latter undertook to pass legislation making French one of the official languages of the Territories, I repeat, one of the official languages. The Government of Canada promised to pay all costs of establishing and providing French services.
That same month, inspired by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Legislative Assembly of the Territories passed Bill 9, which I just quoted, establishing the official languages of the Northwest Territories. The purpose of this legislation was to make institutional bilingualism-I repeat, institutional-official. For the benefit of those who still have trouble understanding the difference between institutional and individual bilingualism, I may recall that institutional bilingualism means giving Canadians access to institutions in the official language of their choice, either French or English. This applies not only to the legislative body but also to the courts. It is also true-this is very important and I will get back to it later on-that there is some concern about the government services that communities are entitled to receive. That is another matter, but I want to make sure the government understands that, when we agree to a second extension, we also want some firm commitments from this government regarding services in French for the Territories' French-speaking communities.
Madam Speaker, the bill that was intended to make NWT government institutions bilingual by January 1, 1988-and I am still referring to the original legislation passed in 1984-extended the deadline until December 31, 1990, following a number of technical difficulties the NWT government encountered with the translation of acts, ordinances, and so forth.
The deadline was extended to December 31, 1990, and now, a month before the extension expires, we are again asked to extend or postpone the deadline, if you prefer, until April 1, 1992. That is the purpose of Bill C-92.

Government Orders
Madam Speaker, as far as translation is concerned, the NWT government has made considerable progress. I am told all its laws have been translated. The ordinances must now be revised, in French and in English, and printed, while regulations adopted pursuant to these ordinances must be updated.
The Liberal caucus, whose spokesman I am today, acknowledges the good will of the Government of the Northwest Territories and appreciates the request made in its ordinance. Given this request, we support the adoption of this bill at all stages today.
Madam Speaker, naive though I may appear, I should like to comment briefly on the situation in the Northwest Territories as it relates to the official languages.
The legislation adoption process and the implementation of such legislation concerning services to the public at large, particularly to the communities, is essential. For too long now the francophone residents of the Northwest Territories have been completely ignored with respect to dealings which concern them, especially the strong impact on the future of their community, its laws, and government services. For too long now, Madam Speaker, their needs have been decided for them without consultation. The message I would convey to the federal government, responsible as it is for protecting, supporting and promoting national unity, is to act as defender and representative of these minorities before the governments of the Territories so that these governments understand that the francophone communities of the Northwest Territories now ask nothing more than to be consulted and involved when governments open up new services, when governments willingly agree to meet the major needs of the residents of the Northwest Territories, one of our country's main regions.
Madam Speaker, when the House passed the Official Languages Act in June 1988, the government was committed to promote the growth of francophone and anglophone minorities. Again I say francophones and anglophones because they do exist. Some minorities are constantly under the threat of assimilation, and I am referring to francophones outside Quebec. But then again Quebec has an anglophone minority that has the right to be there and to enjoy the services to which it is entitled under the Constitution and the law.
As full-fledged citizens of this country which has two official languages we make the following argument, namely that the existence and survival of these francophone groups in the various provinces and in the Territories are linked to the survival of our country itself, and that we have to protect and support these groups to ensure equality and respect between Canada's two linguistic communities.
If we lose our francophone communities outside Quebec, Madam Speaker, what is the point in having bilingual Territories if no one is there to use the law, if no one is there to benefit from government services? What will be the use of balkanizing into two entities, one speaking only French in Quebec and the other speaking only English outside Quebec? This is why it has become imperative for governments, particularly those which have not progressed as much as the Northwest Territories or New Brunswick, for example, or the federal government, to consider the importance of catching up with others. A year or so ago Alberta and Saskatchewan were the scene of rather trying times when their parliaments or legislative assemblies denied the traditional and constitutional rights of people to have laws in French. Following what I would call very regrettable incidents, we came to realize that certain governments remain quite indifferent to these provisions.
Madam Speaker, bearing this in mind, the Liberal caucus, in addition to expressing its support for the Territories and commending them for the gains made by the francophone community so far, would also remind the federal government of the importance of its commitment to promote and support these communities. To a number of people in the north, and to the NWT francophone community as a whole, services are far more important. The need for services is far more pressing. Services are their main priority.
Translations are fine. To have laws and ordinances translated into French is excellent. However, if there are no services to help these communities live in French in the north, all this won't be much use. It will be a purely symbolic gesture.
That is why we want this government to keep its promise to the NWT francophone community and give it the support it needs, so that it can obtain health and education services from the Territorial government-I won't give the whole list, because hon. members know
November 23, 1990

what I am talking about. I am referring to Section 23 of the Constitution which gives Canadians the right to send their children to the school of their choice, either in English or in French. That is not yet the case everywhere in Canada, and it is now eight years since the Constitution was ratified. There are still a number of provinces where it is impossible for a child to be educated in its mother tongue.
We must make up for lost time, Madam Speaker. In three of our provinces, Canadians still cannot speak before a criminal court in the language of their choice. Three provinces have yet to grant this fundamental right of every Canadian to be able to defend himself in the language of his choice. We still have a long way to go, and I think it is incumbent on these provinces to catch up with the rest of the country.
Madam Speaker, as the parliamentary secretary pointed out, in January 1991, the Government of the Northwest Territories will be under a legal obligation to provide government or institutional services in French and English. It will be under the obligation to provide for the use of both official languages in territorial courts, starting January 1991. But will the NWT Government be able to provide those services by that time? I am told that not everything is in place yet, despite this deadline.
Will this government have the technical capacity to meet these legal requirements? Or will we again have a situation where francophone minorities must resort to court challenges in order to defend their rights?
Madam Speaker, I hope we will not always be in a situation where the minority, which sometimes happens to be the weaker party, has to resort to legal remedies to protect its rights.
I make this point for the benefit of the federal government, because it has the resources. It has the money to assist these groups. As for the political will, as I said before, it is there, in the Northwest Territories. So in fact, the Secretary of State merely has to conclude agreements with the Northwest Territories that would ensure the availability of certain services in French, without putting an additional burden on NWT residents.
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, these are matters that are of considerable concern to NWT francophones. It asked me to beg the government, in the course of this debate, to act on a firm commitment, made when the Official Languages Act was passed nearly two years ago, to help these communities defend their language rights.
Finally, Madam Speaker-and I will try to be brieflike all hon. members I realize that the NWT government had to overcome considerable technical difficulties when faced with the enormous task of having all its statutes translated. As I said earlier, I am told that all the statutes have been translated and all that remains are the ordinances and a few regulations.
We are aware that there are a few problems, despite all the good will. For instance, it is not easy to find translators who are familiar with the requirements of legal and legislative translation. We also realize that funding made available by the federal government should continue to be made available to these communities.
Madam Speaker, considering the good faith shown by the territorial government, we are prepared to give our consent to this provision. In concluding, I would like to say, to the people who think this is a waste of time and money, that we feel this provision for the translation of laws, ordinances, regulations and other texts into French is important if we want this country to remain united.
I deplore the attitude of some people in this country, of the authors and writers and groups that say it is a waste of time. If it is worth having two official languages, as we do, it is worth protecting them across this country to achieve language equity. It is also worthwhile to ensure that these groups, these French or Englishspeaking communities, wherever they happen to live in this country, have access to government services, laws and ordinances in their own language. As I said earlier, I deplore the negative approach taken by some people to this question. The game is not over yet, however. I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that unlike what was said by Mr. Yves Beauchemin, a writer, when he appeared recently before the Commission-

The Belanger-Campeau Commission.

Government Orders

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I was looking for the quote. In any case, Mr. Beauchemin said recently before the Belanger-Campeau Commission in Quebec that minorities, that francophones outside Quebec were like a corpse that is still warm.
I would urge Mr. Beauchemin and others of the same persuasion to look beyond their immediate horizons and visit Canada. There are still large groups in this country that want to survive and want this country to survive, and that simply want the majority to give them a measure of equity and exercise some generosity so that we can continue to defend and preserve this country, Canada, that some day, I hope, will be respectful and supportive of both official language groups.
Finally, I would like to say that today, we are prepared to adopt all stages of the bill, including committee of the whole and third reading.

Madam Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I wish to speak today on this bill. I know that the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier is particularly fond of this subject and that he could speak about it for an hour or two even. I heard his speech.
So, as a gesture of goodwill, we are not going to delay the passing of Bill C-92, an Act to amend the Northwest Territories Act, in order to allow more time for the statutes and orders to be translated into French.

As I said, Madam Speaker, the bill will provide bilingual services in the north and will extend the time that the federal government has given to the Northwest Territorial government, which is its creature. It is still a territoiy really. It is really still a creature of the federal government, although some day I hope it will be independent in the sense of being a province.

I am saying this for my friend from the Bloc Quebecois who is going to speak after me. I am anxious to hear his speech.

The original commitment to bilingual services was made in 1985. Given the recent tensions in this country and the Belanger-Campeau commission that my friend
from Vanier spoke about, we do not want the federal government to drag its heels in providing minimal services for the francophone community, francophones hors Quebec, especially the francophone community where the federal government has jurisdiction and where this Parliament has a special responsibility, and that is in the Northwest Territories.
The federation of NWT francophones wrote to the Secretary of State in late October expressing some serious concern about the fact that promises made about services in the French language were not being kept. We would like to see these technical delays overcome and the promises kept. We do not want any excuses. We want the government to provide these minimum services.
Article 23 of the Constitution provides for parent-controlled schooling to the francophone community in the territories where numbers warrant. It is essential that francophones in the territories now be closely consulted in the implementation of this right in the near future. It is also essential that francophones in the territories now be consulted about government services that must be made available to them in their own language.
It is all veiy well to translate laws, but you need medical services, legal services and so on. Although I am from British Columbia, I have lived in the east for 11 years. I travel back and forth really, bi-coastal if you like. I have found that just across the river in Quebec, I can get health services, legal services and so on in the English language.
Having said that, I want to point out that French is only 3 per cent of the Northwest Territories. I am proud that I worked for the Berger commission there about 15 years ago. We did the commission then in English and in French. We had hearings all across the country in English, French, Dene, Loucheux, Slavey, Dog Rib and Inuktitut. If I might be permitted to speak a little Inuktitut, I remember when I was a much younger man, I had a beard and they used to call-
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut]
-which means sick, sick, the little guy with the beard. Those were great days. I remember the territories and I remember the effort to have other languages.
I see my friend from the bloc Quebecois about to speak, and I will end now. I want to tell him and other people, it is with some difficulty that anglophone mem-
November 23, 1990

bers of Parliament from western Canada and other places stand up in this House and advocate francophone rights outside of Quebec. I am sure he realizes that if we adopt his position, and Quebec becomes sovereign, there would not be any anglophone rights outside of Quebec and the new English Canada would be unilingual. I am not saying I would want to see that. I am just saying the reality of it would be that we would be looking at a Quebec which is French and the rest of Canada which is English. There would be no effort like there is here to try to translate laws. That is not a threat. That is a just a statement of reality.
I point out to him-

I point out to my friend that he may perceive things differently, but that this is how Laurier perceived them. So did Henri Bourassa and Pierre Trudeau. He was a member of Trudeau's government. They envisaged a bilingual Canada.

I will say this in English. It is not so much bilingual, but to respect French and English rights throughout Canada. That is what this is about, and that is why we in the New Democratic Party support it. That means to extend francophone rights, even in this case when it is only 3 per cent of the population, where it is a majority native people.
We see it as a society where we respect language rights. We respect the rights of the two founding people because the way in which this country was created-I like to think of it as a cake, with the bottom being the native people, the base, French and English, and then the new multicultural reality of the present. I am sure he has a different view of a different sort of country. I think what we have fought for for almost 150 years is still worth fighting for. I hope that the translators will get going and the government in the Northwest Territories can provide those services in French.

Madam Speaker, after listening to my colleagues' comments on Bill C-62, I must share a few thoughts with you. We are hearing
Government Orders
today speeches on what I would call equal Canada. There are speeches on the principles of bilingualism, and generosity. For years, I believed in that legal fiction. I thought that it could become a reality. However, after all those years and after travelling all over the country, we must come to the conclusion that we are deluding ourselves if we think that Canada is bilingual. In everyday life, bilingualism is a reality only for a small elite in Canada, especially in the National Capital Region.
Madam Speaker, I know that you had the opportunity to travel across the country. I heard Premier Clyde Wells give speeches on our bilingual country. Well, I visited bilingual Newfoundland. The truth is that bilingualism is totally non-existant in that part of Canada.
Madam Speaker, I travelled extensively across Canada and I would say that, all in all, one of the few places in which I found bilingual services was airports. That is to say when you do not arrive late, after the bilingual attendant has left. But, in everyday life, there is no bilingualism.
When I hear my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier tell English Canada that to allow laws to be published in bilingual format in the Northwest Territories is a token of unity, I want to warn English Candians that this is a mirage. Indeed, translating the laws of the Northwest Territories will do nothing for promoting the economic, social and cultural development of Quebec.
Of course, we have always been under the impression that it was normal for governments to provide bilingual services, that it was a vested right in a supposedly bilingual country.
But trying to make English Canada believe that bilingualism is the mainstay of national unity and that it will keep this country whole and united is tantamount to perpetuating a monumental fraud! Bilingualism is there only to respect individual rights, not to convey to Quebecers the message that everything is just fine, see how generous we are, doing you this kind of favour! Madam Speaker, that is an optical illusion in the reality of day-to-day life.
It does hurt at times. I went to Winnipeg earlier this week to adress the Federation of Manitoba Municipalities. A man walked up to the microphone and, referring to bilingualism and the official languages legislation, he asked: "My grandson is learning French, why are you giving up?" I replied: "My dear man, I hope your grandson is learning French for his own cultural better-

November 23, 1990
ment. I hope your grandson is not learning French just to please me!"
I was not posing as Canada's saviour when I learned English, Madam Speaker, I just wanted to be able to communicate with my English-speaking colleagues, to understand both this country and the United States. I find it very hard to remain still every time I see someone trying to hoodwink the public.
In English Canada we often have the impression that they consider bilingual programs to be a major concession to Quebecers. I say to them: Do not look at it that way! Quebecers who have chosen to be bilingual did so for their own personal enrichment, they wanted to learn someting about another culture, and we hope you take a similar approach. We hope that access to the French language-which is considered as being a privilege-will prove to be the long-sought opportunity to open up onto the rest of the world, for we are all citizens of the international community. But do not delude yourselves into interpreting that as a contribution to national unity.
Madam Speaker, let me tell you that when bilingualism becomes the motive for promoting the principle of nation, we cannot get away from the fact that there are two nations in this country, perhaps even three if we include native people. Therefore we have unilingual nations within a supposedly bilingual judicial structure, and bilingual individuals within a minority. But again I emphasize that we cannot equate granting these services with promoting national unity, and that is because people have been fooling themselves for years and years thinking that this kind of gesture has to be a big favour to francophones. If they believe in bilingual institutions, it is not a favour but a right.
Be that as it may, Madam Speaker, you cannot expect Quebecers to haul down their sovereignty banners simply because there is one more translator in the Northwest Territories! That would be creating an illusion, and then some!
All I can say to our francophone friends outside Quebec is that the best anchor they can have is a sovereign and francophone Quebec which will then be a vibrant society of French language and culture. We will always be open and friendly to those who want to live in French, to those who want to raise and educate their
children in French and give them the opportunity to grow up and work in French. When we talk about bilingualism, Madam Speaker, the only truly bilingual city in Canada is Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to respond to allegations made by the Canadian co-operative housing federation and set the record straight.
The Co-operative Housing Program is an experimental program covering a period of five years ending on December 31 this year. It was designed by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in co-operation with the Canadian co-operative housing federation. Initially, the federal government, through CMHC, injected $5 million annually-in addition to an additional budget of $5 million-totalling $30 million over a period of five years. The Minister of State (Housing) has fully honoured his commitments.
The Canadian co-operative housing federation had suggested that CMHC use the indexed mortgage loan formula to finance the projects. However, the federation's forecasts did not materialize, which consequently had a negative impact on the number of housing units delivered. We have tried in every way to help the federation reduce unit construction costs, which would have made it possible to build more housing units, but to no avail. Furthermore, we had to raise the annual subsidy cost to $3,000 per unit because of increased operating and capital costs.

Last year, Canada Post could report $149 million in profits which was made at the expenses of small communities. The people at that meeting sent a clear message to the government: Its postal services privatization, or should I say dehumanization, policy is hurting rural Canada. Post offices are the heart of small communities and closing them is an attack against all the traditions attached to them, not to mention the elimination of many jobs. Canadians, wherever they live, have a right to centralized and humanized postal services like those provided in urban communities.
This government left the isolated communities to fend for themselves. Just think of the cuts in transportation.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to draw, with some enthusiasm, a comparison between the Conservative Parties of Britain and Canada.
As hon. members will know, earlier this week Margaret Thatcher's leadership was challenged. Just yesterday, the Iron Lady realized that her policies and waning popularity in the polls would preclude her party from winning the next general election. She did the honourable thing and resigned.
Perhaps the chief thorn in her side is her new poll tax. This tax has Britons up in arms and protesting in the streets, not too unlike the Canadian reaction to the Conservative's GST.
When a government introduces a tax that has the disapproval of over 80 per cent of the population at the same time as it forces the nation into an economic downturn, it is time to reconsider seriously its leadership and ability to govern.
If only the leadership selection process were the same in Canada, I am certain we would see members opposite lining up for the Prime Minister's job.
Given the incredible similarity, perhaps the Prime Minister should follow the lead of his British counterpart and resign.

Madam Speaker, this Sunday has been called the international day to end violence against women. This is a timely reminder to our government for three reasons.
First, following the second anniversary of this government's re-election, publicizing the violence issue shows what little, if anything, six years of Tory rule have done to improve the quality of life for Canadian women.
Second, approaching the first anniversary of the Montreal students' massacre, publicizing the violence issue shows how hard this social disease can hit if we do not address it sincerely.
There was much hope when a woman was appointed as Minister of Justice. It is now clear with her mishandling of Bill C-80 that she is giving in to the gun lobby.
Third, coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, publicizing the violence issue, which the commission did not even touch, shows how far we have come, yet how far we must still go.
Until this government ceases to believe that all women need is a few appointments to high places in Canada, a woman's work will never be done.

The hon. member across who speaks of peanuts when he is spending the taxpayers' money is simply displaying that same kind of callous disregard for the Canadian taxpayers now that his party showed in the past when the debt rose far beyond what it had ever been in the country.
In addition, as members will know, the supplementary estimates which are tabled here as well indicated additional support for the Department of the Environment, some $78.3 million. In addition to that, the Minister of the Environment will be announcing early in December to the House and to the country the green plan, which will also provide additional resources to the environment throughout Canada.

Madam Speaker, I cannot believe that the hon. parliamentary secretary would raise the green plan, when we all know what is happening to it. The government has shown confusion and terrible weakness in environmental concerns. Rumours abound about the cuts.
Can the minister assure that the green plan is not about to drown in the government's red ink? Can the government assure us that the green plan, as established in the first draft of September, has not suffered dramatic cuts and that they are not reflected here? Will the
Oral Questions
government assure us that the consultation process will be honoured with the environmental community?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
I can assure you, Madam Speaker, and all interested Canadians, that when it is announced in December the green plan will reflect at that particular time the result of consultations which have taken place across Canada, a process of consultations which was never attempted by any other government in Canadian history.
I will also assure you, Madam Speaker, and the hon. member, that there will be before Canada a long-range systematic plan to address the problems of the environment such that his party and his government never even contemplated when they were in office.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. Canadians were told that figures tabled today in the House would clarify the costs associated with the Canadian presence in the Gulf. The supplementary estimates, however, only add to the confusion and contradict other reports.
Can the minister assure Canadians that these costs do not represent an escalation of the Canadian role in the Gulf? Will he further agree, in light of the contradictory information, to request that the Auditor General conduct an immediate and independent review of the cost of our participation in the Gulf?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that, not only are the numbers accurate to the best of our ability, but also that the total cost figures that have been requested for maintaining our presence in the Gulf and for aid to the civil power to the Government of Quebec this summer, has been absorbed within the departmental budget. It is a considerable amount of money.
We have reassigned ship days. We have reassigned flying hours because at this time there is real time training taking place. We have adjusted exercises. At the same time, through the budgets of 1989 and 1990, we

November 23, 1990
Oral Questions
have reduced some $820 million of expenditures this year in the Department of National Defence.
We were very close to the line when these two unexpected crises occurred. Because we were not able to meet our defence budget, we had to approach central agencies due to the unanticipated or unbudgeted expenditures. I am sure that he agrees that this is a very logical and reasonable way to assess the problem of today.

Madam Speaker, Canadians are spending $1.2 billion to maintain our forces in Europe to support a cold war that officially, and practically speaking, no longer exists.
Why is the government forcing Canadians to cut back in spending on necessary domestic programs? Why has the government not reallocated spending from Europe, instead of forcing Canadians here to bear the burden of the Gulf?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member should be aware when he talks about Europe that we are part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We have made adjustments and he asks why we do not make more.
I bring to his attention that the NATO Alliance over the last 40 years has been responsible for the most creative and the most assured way to have a peaceful world by signing the CSCE and the CFE which took place just this weekend in Paris. East and west sat down and came to an agreement to have a more peaceful and more secure world. That, I say to him, is because the NATO Alliance has held firm and strong for the last 40 years.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Treasury Board.
The tabling of these documents in the House today proves to everyone that there is a total lack of financial management in the government.
Right on.

The Prime Minister and his Cabinet met without consultation with Parliament and made the decision to go into the Persian Gulf without knowing how they were going to pay for it. Surely, one goes hand in hand with the other.
Why was the government not as dedicated about providing a financial plan for the Department of National Defence to do its job, as they were to provide for $257 million to prepare for the collection of the most hated tax in Canadian histoiy, the GST?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I draw to the hon. member's attention once again that the Persian Gulf crisis and the aid to the civil power for the Government of Quebec were not able to be planned for.
That is your first responsibility.

The member from Labrador suggests that is one of our first responsibilities. I suggest to him that no government plans for the additional costs of a crisis which could lead to war.
Responsible governments and democracies, when they make a commitment to bring about a more peaceful and secure world, call upon the people and the government to provide the resources so there will be a more peaceful and secure world.

Madam Speaker, the government is demonstrating that it has no plan at all. Ever since the government was elected to power in Canada six years ago, the Prime Minister and a series of defence ministers have been standing up in the House and saying, with great rhetoric, that they are going to provide the money for the Department of National Defence so that our Canadian military personnel can do their job. Instead, the government has cut the budgets of the defence department and left it with an empty cupboard. Now they are robbing other departments to pay for the sins of the financial mismanagement of the government.
Why did the government not keep its commitments to Canada's military forces, to Parliament, and to the people of Canada, instead of once again proving that their promises are not worth the paper they are written on? You let the department down. You know it.

Hear, hear.
November 23, 1990
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot help but smile. I am not sure if the hon. member and his party supports the effort of the Canadian government in providing, along with some 28 other nations, a force in the Persian Gulf area. I know that his leader draws upon that. He says it is not something in which we should be involved. I suggest to him that he knows in his heart that it is something in which we should be involved. He knows full well the difference between capital expenditures and operational requirements. If he does not, I would be pleased to provide him a briefing at the Department of National Defence.

Madam Speaker, Canadians woke up this morning to find that their government was $4.8 billion short. At the same time that this government is cutting $10,100,000 from the communications budget, it is adding $14,305,000 to advertise and communicate its GST. They are robbing Marcel to pay Mike. Why is the government crippling the CBC and the National Archives, among others, to sell Canadians a tax that they despise?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)

I am afraid, Madam Speaker, that the hon. member suffers from an acute attack of misunderstanding. I am explaining through supplementary estimates how the money that has already been voted in the budget is going to be spent. I hope she understands that. This is not an increase. This is a method by which I explain to the House, and I ask authority of the House to spend the money that was already voted upon.
If you take the GST, for example, my colleague can explain and I can explain that in front of the committee we explained that there would be transitional costs. Now we have put the numbers together and we have come to the House at the first opportunity to explain them. This is what it is about. It is not additional funds.
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, you and I understand that sometimes perhaps the government feels that women have difficulty understanding this, but $257 million extra. That seems extra to me. Mind you, it would take an economist, a mathematician and a wizard to follow the estimates that the hon. minister tabled.
Radio Canada International, for example, does its job of connecting Canada to the international community, connecting Canada to its nationals abroad and in particular, connecting Canadians to their loved ones on duty in the Persian Gulf. In this cut to communications, is Radio Canada International the next to go? Will our military soon have no radio link to those at home because of the minister's mismanagement?

Even if some submissions asked that these requirements be maintained in the case of services in isolated areas, the Agency believes that the minister of Transport has exclusive responsibility over that matter. Here is my question: Will the minister have the last word on the issue of VIA Rail, a Crown corporation, cutting passenger services in isolated areas?

Madam Speaker, I can assure my honourable colleague that I will have the last word. It is my responsibility and not the National Transport Agency's, to make the decision about isolated areas.

November 23, 1990

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister to justify why in the estimates under the Department of Finance the government is planning to spend an extra $14.3 million on advertising the GST and why in the estimates under the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs they are going to top up expenditures in the GST information office by an additional $6.5 million.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister, as leader of the government in the House today how he can justify spending almost $21 million extra to advertise the GST in this country? How can he justify that?

The government is asking the Canadian people to cut back on all kinds of programs, when it is cutting $25 million out of the department of employment budget to look after the unemployed in this country. How can he justify spending an extra $21 million to advertise the goods and services tax? What are we going to see? More ads on geese flying around this country? The Prime Minister wrapping himself in the Canadian flag? How can he justify that?

Canadian people the expenditures of advertising the goods and services tax, providing accurate information to the Canadian people, which the hon. member does not do.

Madam Speaker, the government in its news release today announcing total cuts of $350 million worth of essential services to Canadians said: "Adjustments were made to minimize any adverse impact on such things as health and safety".
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Can he truly and honestly say that $9.89 million cuts to the health and welfare budget are safe for the poor, the sick, the elderly and disabled Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I can give the assurance that all essential services will be maintained. What we are trying to do with the bill this morning, Supplementary Estimates, is to ensure program delivery is cost effective. The health and safety of Canadians continues to be our main concern. Social programs will be maintained as announced. Programs for seniors will be maintained. In short, people who need additional assistance from the government will continue to get it today and tomorrow, as they did yesterday.

Madam Speaker, how can you maintain that when you have cut $9.89 million?
The government plans to ask for an additional $250 million to help spread informational propaganda for the goods and services tax, yet has the gall to cut the budget for food inspection systems. Which is more important, I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, the health and safety of the GST, or the health and safety of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member should know that we are not cutting spending for programs. We are not cutting essential services. What we are cutting into-
You're cutting Indian Affairs by $6 million.

-is government expenditures and government operations which are not going to affect the people of this country.
He refers to a figure for advertising the GST. Let me tell him that a large chunk of the money tabled today goes toward social elements of the changed tax from the federal sales tax to the GST by sending out GST credits to over 8 million low and modest income Canadians. This government cares about people. That is why this government is cutting government operations in order to assist Canadian people, particularly those with low and modest incomes.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture. With net farm incomes in the prairies slated to drop to almost zero in the next two years and world grain prices at such an incredibly low rate, the lowest in history, and government cut-backs of some 40 per cent on farm support programs during the last two years, I wonder why the minister is cutting $10 million out of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. Surely with the price of grain on the world markets and the cut-backs that have already taken place it was not necessary to cut this additional $10 million out of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I share the member's concern about the very difficult situation in which the grains and oilseeds producers find themselves. As he knows, this year we have provided emergency assistance. We have provided for a cash flow enhancement program. We are hopefully in the final stages of negotiating an appropriate agreement with the provinces that will bring about a long-term safety net and stabilization program. With the Western Grain Stabilization Act, it is a statutory piece of legislation. It is based upon that. When less money is contributed by farmers, it automatically reduces the level of exposure by the federal government. It is for that reason that it is included in the estimates. It is really a reflection of the way the legislation works. The hon.
Oral Questions
member should support that because it was legislation that was originally brought in by the Liberal government.

Madam Speaker, it seems to me that if funds are removed from the stabilization fund, there is less money to be paid out during the next two desperate years when net farm income on the prairies is slated to go to zero. It is an incredible time to be cutting support programs.
Since the minister raised the issue of the safety net program, there is great concern in the agriculture community as to whether the government is willing to fund that in a proper way so that the premiums paid by the three participants, the federal government, the provincial governments and the agriculture producers, will be shared on an equal basis.
Is the minister prepared to give a commitment today that when that program is implemented that the federal government is prepared to pay its full 33 per cent and not welsh, as it did on the crop insurance program, where it cut back to only 25 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker, I would hope that that could be achieved. That is the position that the federal government has taken in going into these negotiations. I think that has broad-based support from the producers. Unfortunately, some provinces do not support that proposal quite as enthusiastically as I am sure the hon. member does.
To refer back to his question with respect to the WGSA, the hon. member should know and should understand that the government has to conform to the legislation. That is precisely what it is doing.
If there are shortfalls, as I have indicated publicly and in the House today, we are triggering the third level of defence mechanism which will analyse the income shortfalls while at the same time moving the income safety net and stabilization program forward. In the process of this, we will take a look at the income situation and try to respond in an appropriate fashion, as we have before.

November 23, 1990

Madam Speaker, almost to the day one year ago, this House unanimously passed a motion expressing concerns about child poverty and attempting to eradicate it.
I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister how he reconciles the support that was shown for that motion less than a year ago today with the continuing cuts that were made in estimates this morning on social programs for Canadian families, the rise in the use of food banks, the lack of child care facilities for young people across Canada and, perhaps the most disturbing estimation that has been made. In The Toronto Star article of September 21, 1990, and I would like to ask the minister to very simply respond to this: "Native Canadian babies have about as much chance of living beyond their first birthdays as do those in Jamaica and Costa Rica, and are at higher risk than babies in Cuba and Singapore." How does he reconcile that?

Cognizance should be taken of the fact that something like 800,000 people have been taken off the poverty roll since this government came into office.

On Clause 1-

Madam Chairman, I wonder if I might be permitted to put a couple of questions to the parliamen-
November 23, 1990

tary secretary. We have given notice to the parliamentary secretary of the questions we want to raise with him in order to get a commitment from the government.
Just to point out initially, we believe that there can be no further delay in implementing bilingualism in the Northwest Territories Legislature. This is the second extension, and there will be no further extensions.
The federal government strongly urges the Government of the Northwest Territories to undertake to consult closely with the Northwest Territories francophone community on the question of government services in French, the more important concern at the end of the day than translated laws. There is a good deal of concern among Northwest Territories francophones that this deadline extension is the opening wedge in the retrenchment of bilingualism across the board. The minister should assure the House that all that is happening here is technical problems relating to translation.
Finally, I have another point. I would like the parliamentary secretary to respond to them. The federal government expects the Northwest Territories government to undertake to consult closely with the Northwest Territories francophones on the question of implementing Article 23 of the 1982 Constitution which provides for parent controlled French language schools where numbers warrant.
Could the parliamentary secretary respond to these three points? Then we could move on with this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, there were three parts to the hon. member's question.
First, we have received assurances from the officials in the Government of the Northwest Territories that there would be no further delay in implementing bilingualism in the Northwest Territories Legislature. Accordingly, we will not be requested to make any further extensions.
Concerning the second question, I would inform the hon. member that the amendment to the new act will not affect the disposition of the Official Languages Act related to the services to the public in French. It should be clear to everyone that this deadline extension only concerns the translation of laws. It is already stipulated that that extension is due to technical reasons.
Government Orders
Specifically in answer to the members's concern, the federal government expects that the Northwest Territories government will continue its consultations with the francophone minority on the questions of governmental services in French.
With respect to the final question, the Secretary of State has offered, by letter to the Government of the Northwest Territories, the support of the federal government to any initiative giving effect to section 23 rights in the Northwest Territories Act. In the Canada-Northwest Territories bilateral agreement on official languages and education the federal government is committed to consult the official language minority on its needs. That is the position of the government, and we will follow through on that.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise in the House today to speak on Motion No. 23. It is my intention to try and explain my views on this issue.
Before we get into that, I would like to mention my disappointment that Bill C-80, the bill that was before the House, was so hurriedly put together in June and because of all the difficulties with it, all the holes in it, that is, it is such a bad bill, that members opposite have decided that they cannot continue with it because it is not even acceptable to government members.
I would like to read Motion No. 23 to the House. It reads as follows:
That a Special Committee of the House of Commons be appointed to study the subject matter of Bill C-80, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Thriff in consequence thereof;
That the said Special Committee shall have all the powers of a Standing Committee pursuant to Standing Order 108(1); and
That the said Special Committee be composed of eight members, to be recommended by the Striking Committee.
I find this very difficult to understand. On the one hand we have a bill that supposedly had extensive consultation and had been looked at extensively by the Minister of Justice and her department, and on the other hand, because members opposite do not approve of the bill and lind it to be offensive to their constituents and I suggest particularly to rural Canada, the minister has decided to withdraw the bill. If this particular bill had been the subject of wide consultations and the information and the changes in the bill had been put to the Canadian Wildlife Federation, the National Firearms Association and the Ontario Arms Collection Association, members opposite would have realized very quickly that there were difficulties with the bill.
I would like to go through, in chronological order, areas of concern of the bill and also areas of the bill that are acceptable to members like myself who are from rural Canada.
I would like to start with portions of the bill that we find to be very difficult to comprehend. That is the negative aspect of this bill. These are areas that I suggest very strongly the newly formed committee have a mandate to look at. The first area is the belief that changing the sizes of the magazines and clips of particular weapons would enhance and improve the situation. Mass murderers, the criminal element and certain individuals in Canada use certain types of weapons whether they are within the law or not.
If Bill C-80 was to go through, the government would be outlawing over one million clips that are presently being used in Canada. It would also outlaw hundreds of thousands of weapons that are presently being used. These weapons have a built-in magazine. This built-in magazine has more than a five-clip capacity or five-bolt capacity.
I question the wisdom and the reasoning of the Minister of Justice, who presented this piece of legislation. Why does she feel that reducing the size of a clip will stop incidents such as the one that took place in Montreal last year?
Another area that we must look at very seriously is the Firearms Acquisition Certificate which is presently in place. There is a belief that there is a need for two references. I question the reason why one would want to have references, similar to passports, and whether any individual in this country will want to put their name forward to make a social and moral decision on their own. This individual asking to purchase a Firearm Acquisition Certificate and in essence, purchase a gun, is of sound moral and social character.
I do not know how an individual will be able to make that type of recommendation and put his or her name on this certificate. Most gun owners that I know would have great difficulty doing that, because one really cannot, without professional help, make that kind of decision. That is going to make it difficult for many gun owners who are certified and who have gone through the safety course to be able to get the sport rifles that they are looking for.

Another aspect of the bill that I find very difficult in this age of democracy is the ability to change regulations at will by Order in Council. I find that to be very offensive because it does not allow for debate in this House on issues that we, as members of Parliament, really have been put here to debate. Orders in Council on changes of significance to people's lives should always be debated in this House and that deserves to be looked at.
Another aspect is the increase in fees from $10 to $50. It is outrageous to think that we are putting in a category for every single weapon that a Canadian may own. When they resubmit their firearms acquisition certificate renewal they will have to pay $50 for every weapon they own.
Most Canadians who are hunters and sportsmen own a variety of weapons. I suggest that having two, three, four or five weapons of different varieties for different types of sport is going to be very expensive for those individuals if the changes in fees are allowed to go through.
The other change that is very difficult for an individual who is a sportsman to understand is the fact that an applicant must demonstrate a secure place within which to store his or her weapons.
I ask members opposite to explain to me in detail how that will be done because there are millions and millions of Canadians who own weapons. Are we proposing, as this government has with this piece of legislation, to allow some sort of inspector to inspect every home in the land to see if they have secured their weapons and put them in a place where they are stored in a proper manner? Or are we saying that as long as the weapons are locked in a closet or in a particular case, that is perfectly acceptable?
Is the legislation suggesting that we have to purchase a particularly secure case, one built in Canada? Most gun owners have a case worth roughly $2,000. Those particular cases are made of a very durable type of alloy which will not allow individuals to break in very easily. I suggest that that is a good idea for people who can afford it, but most gun owners in Canada do not have the financial ability to purchase such a secure type of case to allow them to store their weapons.
I want to talk a little bit about what is good about the bill. There are some good aspects to this bill. If we had not got into the emotional problems that occur whenever

there is some sort of massacre or something that is disgusting to parliamentarians and Canadians as a whole similar to what took place in Montreal last year, we probably would have come forward with some very good legislation.
Although it has not been passed and given Royal Assent, I find it ironic to think that for years and years we have had on the books the ability to force all Canadians who would like to purchase a weapon to go through a hunter and safety course, or a gun safety course of some kind and have some national standard. I think the safety aspects of the bill are a very good idea and should be implemented.
Obviously we would have to take a look at what the regulations and course would entail. These particular courses would give those Canadians who are first-time gun owners an understanding of just what they are purchasing. That is a very positive aspect of the bill and I think we should take a serious look at improving this part of the legislation.
The other aspect of the bill that is very important is the photo ID that would be put on the FACs. That would make it much easier for individuals who are selling weapons to do their job in checking out the moral and social capabilities of persons owning a weapon.
One of the problems with the bill as it relates to the FAC is that it does not stipulate whether the FAC is going to be for all the weapons. Our belief is that it is just going to be for one individual weapon at a time. Therefore, one might need four or five FACs. I think that has to be looked at very seriously.
With regard to how the bill relates to the firearms safety course, the question that has to be raised and will have to be looked at by this committee is, is this for first-time gun owners or are we going back to square one, making every person who owns a gun in the country take the safety course. There are those in Ontario who have gone through a safety program and there are those in other provinces who have not.
Also, we have to take a look at the 28-day cooling off period. Is this essential for those who already have an FAC in hand now, who are already gun owners, and who have already taken the course to which I have referred? Is it necessary to make them wait 28 days in order to get their renewal of an FAC? If they have already been

checked out by the authorities, can they not just go in and have it renewed instantly?
The other thing I would like to touch on today is the belief that this is truly a discussion between rural and urban Canada. There are some major problems in urban Canada with the criminal element using weapons to the detriment of society. In an area such as northern Ontario where I come from, our largest town has a population of 10,000. Everybody knows everybody and everyone knows everyone who hunts and fishes and is a sportsman. It is not so easy in an environment such as that to explain to people that, "No, you cannot have a 10-bullet clip any more. You have to have a five-bullet clip because the other will do someone harm. You have to remove five bullets out of the clip." That argument is very difficult to make.
We seriously have to understand that in rural Canada we do not understand some of the difficulties that are taking place and for what urban Canada is asking. If we asked it of just the different cities in the country having difficulty with the criminal element related to the use of assault weapons that are out there, then we could understand that. But we cannot understand saying this simply because there are difficulties in Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and Halifax, when in the rest of rural Canada there are legitimate gun owners who are very conscientious. They have taken the safety courses, are respectful of the law, and try to maintain the type of respect that I think a gun owner should have.
What I am basically talking about is attitude. There is a fundamental difference in attitude with regard to weapons between people in rural Canada and urban Canada. There is a much larger respect for weapons in rural Canada than there is in urban Canada. The reason for that very simply is because we have grown up with them. It is like suddenly telling an Inuit in the north, where there are no roads, that there is now a road and he is now going to be responsible to drive a car. That individual would have a lot of difficulty with that. That situation is very similar to what we are discussing here.
I am not suggesting for one minute that we cannot improve our gun legislation or that we cannot try, as legislators, to put a stop to the situations that have been taking place. However, for the life of me, I cannot understand how this particular piece of legislation will stop the criminal element and the insane element in our
society from doing what they have been doing. The fact remains that those individuals, who are quite prepared to break the laws of society, will not adhere to this legislation any more than they adhered to the legislation currently on the books. It is very important for us to try to differentiate between the two because if we do not then we are reacting purely on emotion and it will not stop the inevitable from happening.
I would like to come to a conclusion and look at some of the aspects that possibly were not entertained in the drafting of Bill C-80. That is the effect of changing laws on the tourism industry.
The semi-automatic guns that we are talking about that are legal at this time are used throughout North America. When and if this piece of legislation ever goes through, it will also restrict those who use them in the United States of America. Those individuals come to Canada to hunt and fish. Now they will be restricted by our laws and, therefore, our tourism industry will also be affected.
Are we to tell an individual coming across the border that he can no longer use a 10-bullet clip. He cannot use a 308 that has a built-in magnum that will allow for more than five shells. There are hundreds of thousands of weapons like that out there now.
Those are serious considerations that have to be looked at in rural Canada. I know they do not affect urban Canada whatsoever, but they do affect the economy of Canada as a whole. I think we have to seriously look at that.
I am veiy pleased that, in a roundabout way, the minister and the members opposite, whom I know lobbied very heavily on behalf of their own constituents, have asked to have this bill removed and sent back so they can have a true dialogue.
We cannot just get into the emotion of the mass murders that take place. It is very easy for members to stand up and use that as an argument to ban all weapons in Canada. If we are going to use that argument, we will not advance the debate at all as to what is appropriate and what is not appropriate for Canadians.
As a rural Canadian, and as a member who has hunted and owned guns for many years, who has taken safety courses, and who knows that there is a lot more to this than what some members are suggesting, I am very

pleased that it is going to go to committee so we can look at it in a very sane way. With some luck, we can put some legislation in place that will have an effect on what we truly would like to do as members of Parliament. That is to try and stop the criminal element in urban centres from breaking the law.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to take part in this debate on the motion. I think that what we have to make clear for those who are watching on their television sets is that this is a motion to refer Bill C-80, the gun control legislation, to a special committee.
It is in fact a parliamentary device to withdraw the gun legislation, not as the previous speaker would have indicated, that if we passed this legislation it would go into legislative committee where the fine tuning to which he was referring to could take place. Oh, no. What we are seeing here is a parliamentary device, headed up by the Minister of Justice, to withdraw gun control legislation.
There was much hope when the Minister of Justice was appointed, the first woman Minister of Justice. There was a hope that finally things were going to be different; that she would bring a woman's perspective to her duties as Minister of Justice, a different perspective; and that she would be able to put that perspective on to all legislation that came before the House. Those hopes have been dashed, first will Bill C-43, the abortion legislation, and now with Bill C-80. What this parliamentary device, by putting it before a special committee, shows is that the Minister of Justice is caving in to the gun lobby.
I know the Minister of Justice received a lot of favourable comment when she visited the Ecole Polytechnique in April and met with the students and the faculty who had proposed tough gun legislation. It must be recalled that the tragedy at the Ecole Polytechnique on December 6, 1989, was the impetus, she said, for Bill C-80, which would create stiffer gun control legislation.
As I said, she received favourable comment that finally there was going to be stiff gun control legislation. I think that because she is not doing what was hoped would happen, giving a woman's perspective, I will.
I want to point out some of the statistics that relate to guns and women and the difference between the statistics for men and for women. This is why it is important that a woman's perspective should be brought to this debate. Almost exclusively the problems with guns involve men. Women only own a miniscule percentage of guns in Canada. Men constitute the armed part of our society, do most of the shooting and have the greatest chance of being victimized by a gun.
In addition, every poll taken on the issue in Canada and the United states shows that women are the strongest advocates for strict gun control laws. The following statistics should be noted. Only 77 women killed themselves with firearms against 1,047 men. Those statistics are from 1987. Accidental shooting deaths, this is once again 1987 statistics, were 4 women and 56 men. But women do represent one-third of gun victims classified
November 23, 1990

as homicides. In other words, the only category of statistics where women represent a significant percentage is that of murder victims. I think this explains in part why Canadian women overwhelmingly support tougher gun control laws. Therefore, the Minister of Justice, the first woman Minister of Justice, is sabotaging her own bill by this motion, putting it forth into a special committee and is letting Canadian women down, once again. We have seen the chronology of events from 1978 when the last gun control law was passed in this House of Commons. In that legislation there were provisions enforcing mandatory firearms training. However, here we are in 1990 and those provisions have never been implemented. Who are we to believe when the government says now that it will have a program in place by April 1991?
The women of Canada have lost confidence in this Minister of Justice, who came in with such fanfare to her new role. The tragedy that occurred on December 6, 1989 in Montreal serves notice that there have to be tougher gun control laws. I know in my riding we have the phenomena, because it is close to the American border, of American tourists bringing in handguns in their luggage on coming across the border because that is the way they do things there. It is sort of part of your wardrobe to have a handgun. Well it is not like that here, not yet, not in my riding, although I have heard that there are parts of Canada, particularly in the major urban centres, where firearms and handguns are a major threat. Women are the deficit members of society with regard to handguns.
I would urge that the Minister of Justice forget this special committee, forget the stalling tactics, forget caving into the gun lobby and bring forth this legislation so that it can be debated, it can be fine tuned, and we can talk about the debate between rural Canada and urban Canada in a real legislative committee. The stalling tactic is clear. The government is filibustering its own bill. The Minister of Justice has lost control of her bill because she is caving in to her caucus members.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak on this motion. I am as distressed and upset as I think many of us are with regard to the emotion and, perhaps I would go so far as to say, the manipulation that has tended to surround this issue in the past 12 months.
Canada has always had better gun control legislation than its neighbour to the south. There is no question. However, as our modern society evolves and becomes increasingly more violent, it has become increasingly clear to all of us that more gun control and stiffer gun control legislation is absolutely essential if we are to maintain lawful and safe societies, particularly in our cities.
I say that I stand with some misgivings because there is no question that the events of last December 6 at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal were horrific and tragic. They involved the death of 14 young women at the hands of a man who was particularly enraged at young women who broke tradition and entered professions where women were perhaps not so used to being.
The manipulation of these events is something of which none of us should be guilty. In the House on the days immediately following the tragedy there was unity, horror, sorrow, and sympathy for the victims and their families. However, there is no question that in the wake of the events at Ecole Polytechnique came this legislation, this Bill C-80, to make gun control laws in Canada safer and more stringent.
My great difficulty, as it frequently is for those of us on this side of the House, is trying to follow the trail of bread-crumbs set down by the government as to where this bill is going to go. This bill needs to be discussed. It needs to be changed. It is a flawed bill. However, it
Government Orders
does-and I will make mention it further along in my remarks-have some things that are absolutely necessary, if we are to maintain an orderly and safe society in this country.
What is the government's agenda on this bill? Is this bill going to come back to this House? Is it ever going to get to a legislative committee? Is it ever going to be law? Somehow the majority of us on this side of the House think that is unlikely. What we think is that the government has decided this bill is unpalatable to a number of its own back-benchers and that the gun control laws it has introduced are too stringent. Consequently it wants a safe place for this bill to die.
With regard to the subamendment of my colleague for Saanich-Gulf Islands, I disagree with her merely on the question of process. If this special committee holds hearings publicly and really does its work, it will consider the questions, concerns and fears about this bill, of what it does or does not do, it will keep this crucially important subject before the Canadian people and put more pressure on the government.
However, I do have the definite feeling that we are going to be back to square one and that this bill, as we know it, will probably disappear from this House, never to return in its current form.

There are certain similarities between this bill and the bill that you and I, Madam Speaker, know far too well, which is Bill C-43, the abortion bill. One of the problems with Bill C-80-and we do say that the bill does not go far enough-not coming in is that it does nothing about the fact that there are 1,400 gun related deaths every year in Canada. Of these 1,400 gun related deaths, 1,100 are firearm suicides. We also know that tragically the question of suicide is one that relates very intrinsically to the question of disturbed young people. We know that that is where the suicide statistics are among the highest.
We do not have the same problem with guns that the Americans do. We are lucky in that, but we have to act now if we are to ensure that our country does not slide down the same slippery slope. We are subject to many of the same pressures, many of the same urban alienating aspects of life as the Americans. It is said that there are more guns in the city of Detroit than there are people. I do not think we would want that to be said about the city of Windsor. I do not think we would want it to be said about Montreal. We certainly would not want it to be said about Halifax. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, not to make light of this, probably in Halifax my constituents could not afford guns, given the economic situation.
