Let us be sensible about this, even this government is not in the business of outlawing people per se. We are always going to have people, one hopes; we do not always have to have guns.
I admit that I have an overwhelming prejudice against guns. It is part of my background. I come from an urban background. I did not grow up in a house where guns were even in evidence. I do understand that in the rural communities of this country, there is a different outlook. I understand and I sympathize with that but the kind of gun control we are talking about is, in my belief, the kind that can co-exist between the urban fear of increased violence and increased gun usage and the rural tradition of a sane, sensible, orderly and lawful use of firearms for hunting, animal control and whatever.
In conclusion, I want to say that I am disappointed in this government. I am disappointed in the parliamentary secretary and I am disappointed in the Minister of Justice because I think their agenda is the removal of this bill. I think this bill will not come back to the House of Commons. I fear that if we are to see gun control in the life of this Parliament, we will have to start all over again. I think that would be a shame because there are things in Bill C-80 that are good. There are things in Bill C-80 that the Canadian people want, my constituents want them and the people right across this country want them. If my premonitions are true, and I suspect they are, then shame on the government for not having the courage of its convictions, shame on the minister, shame on the parliamentary secretary.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter into this debate today and to offer some views with respect to this important subject matter.
A couple of the hon. members who just spoke, particularly the hon. member for Halifax, have implied that there was a lobby among some members of the government party that got this piece of legislation sent to a committee and, as a result of that, it would be swept under the rug, and therefore not lead to the conclusion that Canada would have effective gun legislation.
I can inform her, through you, Mr. Speaker, that I would be one of those members who has lobbied to have another look at this legislation, but I certainly would never be a member who would lobby to say that we should have no legislation or that we should have weak or ineffective legislation.
I believe that there are two constituencies with two different perspectives on this important issue. The bill just tabled tends to satisfy one of those constituencies. I say that it is possible to have good, effective, workable legislation that will satisfy both of the two polarized views with respect to guns.
When the hon. member for Halifax addressed the House, she made a comment that could not help but have me reckon back to the truth of what she said. She said that we have to look at guns differently in urban areas than in rural. I do not subscribe to the "have to" part of that, but I do subscribe to the cultural difference that exists between those two situations.
I was a member of the House some many years ago when the Liberal government was introducing its gun legislation. The heat was coming into this Chamber from all parts of the country. It was during the highest period of tension on gun control and rural Canada in that all of its regions was mad. I was struck by the fact that as I drove into the community of Hanna, Alberta, coming out
Government Orders
of the Big Country Sporting Goods Store was a person carrying a new rifle. He walked just in front of where I had parked my car. Several people stopped on the sidewalk to examine his new rifle. They pointed it in the air. They moved the workings of it and praised this fine new rifle that he had. Then, the person went on, put it in his truck, and went back out to the ranch.
That was a very comfortable situation about which any urban person would have been struck by the casualness of that sort of conversation. Had that happened on Yonge Street in Toronto, four blocks of citizens would have absolutely evaporated. Somebody pointed a rifle in the air, handed it over to his friend, showing it back and forth, and these ranchers were thinking absolutely nothing other than one of them had purchased a new tool to his industry.
I come from that kind of countiy. I know there are colleagues in all three parties from those remote regions of Canada. In the Peace River area of British Columbia, one is probably a moose hunter. In Canada's two northern territories, one's livelihood and security is largely dependent on it. Wrestling polar bears by hand is largely fictional. It may make covers of men's magazines, but do not ask anyone in the high North to do it.
For personal security, for food supply, and in the ranching and farming industries, it is a tool of the industry. I am a fruit farmer, Sir, and rabbits can cause a lot of difficulty to my orchards. The presently proposed legislation would like to have it limited to a five-bullet clip in the gun. Those who know me at all know it takes more than five bullets for the rabbit to start getting scared when I go after them. I obviously need more than a five-bullet clip.
I submit that we really need to redress the thought processes on this legislation. From the earliest of examination by the Government of Canada, the community of Canada that drafted the legislation was largely urban, but not totally. It then submitted it to the justice ministers of both past and present governments. They came to the notion of gun control from the perspective that the gun is evil, that it is the instrument that is wrong,

November 23, 1990
Government Orders
and that it is the instrument that we somehow have to do something about.
The automobile also kills many people. We have had as a society a more mature attitude about how we regulate the automobile. We do not start from the perception that the automobile is wrong. We start from the perception that we will train the operator through written and oral examinations, and then in skill testing. I believe that ought to happen also with the gun.
One ought not to be able to use a gun unless able to demonstrate competence. One should be required to demonstrate competence not only on physical skill, but on mental security. I believe that those persons to whom I have spoken-members in gun organizations or those who use guns as a means to their livelihood-would subscribe to that.
As a member of Parliament from a rural region of Canada, I can tell you, Sir, that I do not desire, any more than any urban person anywhere, to have a gun in the hands of a lunatic. But there is that funny notion that when these awful, tragic, deplorable, emotional situations take place in our country, such as that at Ecole Polytechnique about a year ago, that somehow if we attack the instrument, we will achieve justice. The person who committed that crime was mad. Everything about him demonstrated that he was a person filled with anger. It would be naive in the unfortunate extreme for us to presume that, had we at some earlier period of time abolished every gun in the country, the crime would not have taken place in some other way. I know that statistics do not in any situation necessarily establish proof.
With regard to training and skills, I would give the example of Switzerland. Because Switzerland does not have an armed forces as such, but requires that every male aged 18 and over must have a high powered rifle in their possession and be trained to use it. They undergo training. One of the things that is observable about Switzerland is it has one of the western world's lowest incidences of crimes with a gun and yet it is a nation in which virtually every home has a gun. I submit that what has been wrong through a history of almost 20 years now is that we have approached this issue from the perspective that we have to control the gun, rather than to somehow control licensed safe operation of the person.
The other area that I wish to mention is that, for those regions of the country where guns are used in the line of work or as a tool to a livelihood, ambiguity in the regulatory process causes a great concern. People know who the regulators are and they know it is largely urban Canada. It is the bureaucrats of Ottawa. They are very fine people and many of them are very, very hard working, but there are not many people in the rural and northern regions of Canada who believe that their views will be expressed in a change in the regulation. They want a consultative process that designs the right legislation and fixes it specifically.
If we leave lots of changes for the regulatory process, where many things can be changed at whim, it will never be changed with the consultation of rural Canada. That fear must be set aside. I say to you, Sir, it is not difficult to set it aside.
I am absolutely convinced of it and I am pleased that we have been effective in asking the minister to go one consultative process further in an attempt to draft legislation that, on the one hand will make urban Canada say that this is safe and this is good, and on the other hand those who use a gun in of their day-to-day lives will also come to the conclusion that this is acceptable, that this is reasonable, and that we can endorse it. I am fully convinced that that kind of balance can be achieved.
The first objective should be to set aside the notion that it is the instrument that is wrong and come to a far higher and more intense training in the skills and the use, and the testing of the persons competence, both mentally and physically, to use that weapon. When we do, hopefully, we will have a safer society and a more trusted one for all sectors of our country.

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise and speak about the merits and the shortcomings of Bill C-80.
Specifically today, we are speaking on a motion to refer the bill to a legislative committee for further study.
It seems that the Tory caucus has reached the Minister of Justice. As a former president of the Dover Rod and Gun Club, I bring certain strong views to the subject of gun control. I am a hunter and sportsman, as are many of my constituents. It is economically important to my riding that hunting is allowed. I am of the firm belief that any gun control legislation must not hinder the honest citizen, that the current laws on the books should be used to the fullest against the dishonest citizen.
It is estimated that there are six million guns in Canada today. Canadians can buy firearms and ammunition at more than 10,000 outlets across Canada. Those figures may startle those who favour tougher gun control, but the figures show Canada does not have a high homicide rate or a high gun use.
The laws that are on the books now should be enforced by the police and the judicial system. We have a strong gun law in Canada today. It is not being enforced.
A strict system of controls was first introduced by the Liberal government in 1977 in order to prevent the criminal and irresponsible use of firearms and to encourage responsible gun ownership and use.
I have received many letters from constituents who are hunters like myself. One, in particular, the Kent Clover Leaf Conservation Club has some serious concerns with the bill that I share. For example, the proposed limitation of magazine capacities to five rounds on semi-automatics is unacceptable to the club, and it was mentioned earlier by the previous speaker. Guns are designed for
November 23, 1990

certain clips and a five-clip in an automatic is of very little use.
They also stand in opposition to any further restrictions to or the banning of semi-automatic rifles, pistols or shotguns. Again, it does nothing to deter crime, but only hinders the enjoyment of a legitimate sport. Those who know nothing of guns or sport shooting are quick to offer that sport shooters do not need the new technology of self-loading firearms. It must be pointed out that they have been on the scene since the turn of the century and are an important part of sport shooting, in fact, also of the Olympics.
In the town of Wallaceburg, which is in my riding, we have the Lee-Enfield rifle in the museum. This gun under the new legislation would be banned. This gun has been known all over the world and has been used in two world wars.
The club makes some good points and I want to quote from their letter to the Minister of Justice on June 26, 1990:
The criminal aspects of gun use must be tightened and enforced.
Murder, armed robbery, assault with or without a weapon and the
possession of a firearm or ammunition at a public gathering are all
illegal.
So, we do have the law, but it is not being upheld by the judicial system.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   NORTHERN QUEBEC REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL CONSTITUENCY
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   NORTHERN QUEBEC REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should introduce legislation to provide an additional constituency in Northern Quebec which would be identical to the territory covered by the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement of 1975 and thereby provide better representation for the people of Northern Quebec and, in particular, for the Inuit, Cree and Naskapi citizens who are the majority in this area.
He said: Madam Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to provide a new constituency in the extreme north of Quebec where the great majority of the population is Cree, Inuit or Naskapi. The area for the constituency that I have in mind is the area which would be more or less similar to the area covered in the James Bay Agreement of 1975.
In 1975 a land claim settlement was arrived at with respect to the Cree and the Inuit living in the north of Quebec. It was followed a few years later by a companion agreement with respect to the Naskapi who live on the more eastern side of the same territory.
At the present time, these aboriginal people living in the north of Quebec are not properly represented. I am not saying that the individual members of Parliament who represent those constituencies are bad members of Parliament, but they do not truly reflect the people who live in the far north of Quebec.
Right now in this area there are two constituencies. One of the constituencies, Manicouagan, is on the eastern side of that territory and runs from the St. Lawrence River right up to Hudson Strait and includes the more southern communities-one can call them southern in respect of that area but they are quite north-of Sept-Iles, Port-Cartier, Baie Comeau, and so on.
The majority of the population in the Manicouagan riding is in the southern part of that constituency, near the St. Lawrence River. Consequently the control of the constituency is with those people who are traditional Quebecois people and not aboriginal people.
The other constituency, which is on the western side of the area, is the constituency of Abitibi. It includes the southern communities of Rouyn, Noranda, Val d'Or, and so on. These communities, as well, control what happens in that constituency of Abitibi, and the people in the far north have very little to say.
Rather than have two constituencies which run right up to Hudson Strait and which are divided by a line that runs north and south, I am suggesting that we cut off the northern part of Quebec with a line that would run east and west and form a new constituency which would more or less include the same territory as the territory of the James Bay Agreement. The Quebecois cities of Sept-Iles, Baie Comeau, Port Cartier, Rouyn, Noranda, Val d'Or, and so on, would be south of that constituency and would belong to properly composed traditional Quebec constituencies.
I am not proposing that we take away one of the constituencies now allocated to Quebec for this purpose. Right now Quebec has 75 seats. I am suggesting that we have a 76th seat to deal with this very special need and very special proposal. Of course such a constituency would have fewer than the average population of most constituencies in Canada. The population would be more or less 20,000 people north of that line. By the way, that line would run near the 52nd parallel.
I must point out that in a sense it would be equivalent to the new constituency of Labrador, which is now a single constituency. Since 1988 the constituency of Labrador does not contain any territory on the island of Newfoundland, and that is new since 1988. It was done for the same purposes as I am suggesting now for the north of Quebec, but the southern boundary of this new
November 23, 1990

constituency would be more or less the same as the southern boundary of Labrador. This sort of exception for constituencies has been done before. We did it in 1988 for Labrador. Before 1988 Labrador was lumped in with a large number of communities on the island of Newfoundland, but it was decided for cultural, historical and community purposes to give Labrador its own constituency.
It was also done, I cannot remember the exact year, for the present constituency of Nunatsiaq. Nunatsiaq is that part of the Northwest Territories on the eastern side which is above the tree line and which contains principally a population of Inuit people. A few years ago we decided, despite the fact that this area had a very small population compared to other Canadian constituencies, that it was appropriate to give the people in that area a representative in Parliament. It was agreed that we would set up this new constituency of Nunatsiaq. I will put on the record the population of that area.
It was also done when we first established the constituencies of Yukon and the Northwest Territories, because we would never have constituencies in Yukon or the Northwest Territories-and here I am talking of the western Arctic, the area around the Mackenzie River-if they were based on numbers of constituents. If we were to be very strict with respect to the number of constituents required for a constituency, then the Yukon, Western Arctic or Nunatsiaq do not meet that criteria. They are way below that criteria, but we did it because we felt that those people needed representation in Parliament and should not be lumped in with the more southerly areas of Canada which have larger populations. By the way, these southerly areas are economically, socially and culturally quite different in many respects and would not really represent the more northern areas.
We also make exceptions for Prince Edward Island. In the Constitution of 1867 we decided that Prince Edward Island should also have the same number of members of Parliament as senators. Consequently Prince Edward Island has four constituencies even though, according to the average Canadian standard for constituencies, there should be only one and a half constituencies in that province.
Private Members' Business
I would like to put on record some of the populations of these areas. For example, right now the constituency of Labrador has about 28,000 people and about 17,000 electors. I would have you compare that with the average Canadian constituency.
For example, let us take the two constituencies that presently exist in the north of Quebec. The constituency of Abitibi has a population of nearly 87,000 people with an electorate of 61,000. I am rounding off the figures. The constituency of Manicouagan has a population of a little over 57,000 people with nearly 39,000 electors. Labrador has a population of 28,000 with 17,000 electors, the Yukon has a population of nearly 24,000 with 16,000 electors, Nunatsiaq has a population of 19,000 with a little over 11,000 electors and the Western Arctic has a population of 32,000, with 18,000 electors.
If we look at the four constituencies in Prince Edward Island, Cardigan, Egmont, Hillsborough and Malpeque have populations of 29,000, 34,000, 31,000 and 30,000 respectively. As I say, we can easily see that these are all much less than the average for Canadian constituencies, which is around 60,000 to 70,000 people in each constituency.
We have done it in the past. We did it for Labrador and Nunatsiaq because we thought it would be a good thing for a group living with the same type of economy to have the right to representation in Parliament.
I should also point out, because it is very instructive, that at the time of Confederation in 1867, when this country was first established, there were 182 constituencies. The average population at that time of each constituency was 17,400. We were able to carry on quite well as a country and our members of Parliament were able to represent those areas quite well.
I gave you the populations for the constituencies of Abitibi and Manicouagan, Madam Speaker, but the national average population for constituencies in Canada is 85,794, and the average for Quebec is 87,099. What I am proposing is, of course, an exception to the rule, but it is not an exception to the rule that has not been done before.
I do not think anyone will deny that we need more aboriginal representatives in this House. We already have two in this party, one from the Northwest Territories and one from Nunatsiaq. I doubt if we would have them if we had stuck to the general rule for populations for constituencies. If we did not have those special

November 23, 1990
Private Members' Business
constituencies with smaller populations than the average, if we did not have them in Nunatsiaq and the Eastern Arctic, we would not have the two members that we now have in this party. There is a member of the Conservative Party from Alberta, a treaty Indian, who comes from an ordinarily constructed constituency, and it is good that he does represent that area, but again, I think we need to do more to involve these peoples in our parliamentary process.
One way of doing it is to carve out constituencies in the northernmost parts of our provinces, such as I am suggesting, where there is a heavier than usual concentration of aboriginal people. It is very difficult for aboriginal people, who are a minority, to be elected in more southerly constituencies. It was done by the hon. member in the Conservative Party to whom I have just referred and it was done on this side of the House a few years ago when Senator Len Marchand was elected in the constituency of Kamloops.
If we look at the situation last summer, where we had a severe crisis at Oka, Quebec with respect to the Kanesa-take community, there was nobody to really represent those people here in Parliament. Many of us tried to represent them. I did, and others did as well, but there was nobody from that community itself. With respect to Kahnawake, it is sad to say but the member of Parliament for La Prairie took very opposite views to the people of Kahnawake. As a matter of fact, the member for La Prairie suggested that the whole population of the Kahnawake community be moved to Labrador or some such place. I do not think that was a good idea.
No matter what we might think of Elijah Harper's politics, while many of us might have supported the Meech Accord and were upset that it did not succeed, we have to admit that the fact that Elijah Harper was in the Manitoba legislature representing a northern constituency in Manitoba helped him represent the views of his people. Whether or not we liked the outcome, the fact that Elijah Harper was in the Manitoba legislature in a minority Parliament meant that he was able to represent the views of his people. I think that is very important.
If you are not in Parliament where you can legitimately put forward the views of your people, in this case
aboriginal people, then you will very often have extraparliamentary action and that action is not always legal or appropriate. You have demonstrations, you have blockades, you have all sorts of things that might happen if you cannot legitimately pursue your views through the ordinary democratic process of elections and Parliament. People get frustrated because they feel they are not being represented in Parliament and therefore they take our their frustrations in other ways to get their political views known. I do not think that is a good thing.
I see here today the hon. member for Abitibi who is one of the most active members on the government side and one of the most active backbenchers in Parliament. I am not suggesting that he be replaced. I am suggesting that it would be more appropriate that he represent the communities that he comes from in the more southern part of the Abitibi riding and, as I said, that we add an additional riding to Quebec to take care of the area that is north of the communities, the Quebecois communities as opposed to the Cree and the Inuit communities which are in the north.
I am familiar with those communities because I was a former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and I visited that region several times. I know that there is a real difference between the Cree, Inuit and Naskapi communities and the communities of Sept lies, Port Cartier, Baie Comeau, Rouyn, Val d'Or, Amos and all the other communities which are non-aboriginal communities and for the most part reflect different cultural, economic and social values, not totally but enough to require special representation in Parliament.
I was responsible as minister for putting through the James Bay legislation in this House. We finally passed it in 1977. Since that time, there has been great development in these aboriginal communities in the north of Quebec. They have their economic development programs, their own school boards and their own health programs. In the Inuit areas there is the Makivik Corporation, the Kativik regional government and so on. It is only appropriate that we give these people some means of being directly represented in Parliament and this is my proposal.
November 23, 1990

Ideally, there should be two constituencies in that area because there are two or even three aboriginal groups. There is the Cree community, which has its own way of life. Then there is the Inuit further north in then-own communities. If we can get agreement to move forward, it would be a great accomplishment. For example, in the western Arctic, which is represented by my colleague from Yellowknife, who is a Dene Indian, her constituency also has some Inuit. There are white people as well, people from different backgrounds. The great majority of people in that constituency are either Indian or Metis or Inuit. The overwhelming percentage of the population is of aboriginal background.
I have been campaigning for this proposal for several years. I have written to the Chief Electoral Officer who, in principle, does not oppose it. This is an idea that came to me from leaders in the north of Quebec. People from the Makivik Corporation and people from the Cree communities felt that this was the only way that they would ever get represented in Parliament. Some of them have run for office before in the constituencies of either Manicouagan or Abitibi as independents, but did not have any chance at all. Their population cannot compete with the populations in the southern part of the constituency.
This is a motion and not a bill. I am asking the House to approve, in principle, the formation of a new constituency in the north of Quebec. This constituency would be more or less contiguous with the territory of the James Bay agreement so that the people in that area could be represented, need not be, but would most likely be represented by an aboriginal person from that area.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   NORTHERN QUEBEC REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Nar-kurmik Marialuk. I rise today to speak on motion M-415 presented by my honorable colleague, the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, proposing that the federal government introduce legislation to provide an additional constituency in Northern Quebec. This new constituency would be identical to the territory covered by the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement of 1975, and would provide better representation for the people living in this large northern area.
Private Members' Business
Madam Speaker, the constituency of Abitibi covers an area of 553,837 square kilometers, or 213,837 square miles, and has a population of 86,990. It is the largest constituency in all ten provinces after the Northwest Territories, and it covers a substantial part of that agreement's territory together with the constituency of Manicouagan, represented here by Charles Langlois. Rest assured, Madam Speaker, we do not intend to replace the member who is here today, because since his arrival in 1988, he has defended the interests of all of his constituency, north and south.
Numbering 3,584, the Inuit are scattered in the following villages: Salluit, Ivujivik, Akulivik, Povungnituk, Inukjuak, Umiujaq, Kuujjuarapik, and Mailasikkut.
Some 9,593 strong, the Crees are scattered in the villages of Whapmagoostui, Chisasibi, Wemindji, East-main, Nemaska, Waswanipi, Waskaganish, and Mistassini.
On February 8, 1983, Mr. Jean-Jacques Martel, of Amos, who has been a member of Parliament here in Ottawa, appeared before the Electoral Boundaries Commission, and said: "As another practical suggestion, the great northern Quebec area, also known as New Quebec or the Ungava Territory, should make a separate electoral riding because of its enormous size, its scattered population, its needs and problems which are different from ours and those of the major metropolitan centres".
During hearings held on December 1, 1986, Mrs. Jeannette Dupuis Lessard, speaking on behalf of the Abitibi-Temiscamingue Regional Development Council (CRDAT), stated similarly: "The climatic and soil conditions which exist in the southern part of the Abitibi riding allows such economic activities as agriculture, forestry and mining, which is clearly not the case of the Middle and Far North of the riding. Do you realize, Madam Speaker, that there is a distance of 1,600 kilometres between the south and the north of my region, which is about the same distance as between Val d'Or and Tampa, Florida. You can understand the time it takes to cover such an area and what enormous task it would be for one member.
The northern part of this territory is inhabited by Natives, Crees and Inuits, with a culture and both social and economic needs different from those of the south. Transport and communication are very difficult. There is no longer any road to the north of James Bay and the airplane is the only means of transportation to visit this

November 23, 1990
Private Members' Business
whole territory. The inhabitants of the middle North and the far North are our neighbours and our social and economic ties with them are increasing. Yet, the CRDAT representative added: "Because of its peculiarities, this northern territory should have its own electoral representative in the House of Commons."
The current incumbent of the Abitibi seat and his predecessors have done everything possible to represent this huge territory. Yet, it must be recognized that such a task is beyond human capacity.
That is why the CRDAT is in favour of the creation of a third electoral riding which would represent the inhabitants of both the middle North and far North of the current Abitibi riding. In view of the small number of its inhabitants, it is true that the creation of such a new electoral riding would not meet the current electoral standards.
But you must realize, members of the Commission, that this electoral ratio does not reflect the reality of the huge and sparsely populated northern territories.
In short, we wish that that portion of the territory be made into an extraordinary electoral district, as defined in the Canada Elections Act and as is the case for the Northwest Territories of Canada.
Madam Speaker, the message from every Quebec electoral district boundaries commission is the same: "Some findings based on geographical or ethnic considerations suggested that the commission should establish electoral districts with less than the minimum population requirement. That was the case of requests received from Inuit and Cree people. Of course, the commission does not have any authority to act on these requests."
Madam Speaker, let us not forget the residents and workers of the La Grande complex, a hydro development with various sites in Radisson, LG1, LG2, LG3, LG4 and elsewhere, as well as the residents in northern communities.
The Cree-Naskapi Commission, chaired by the honourable Justice Rejean F. Paul, from the Superior Court, recommended in Chapter 3 of its 1988 report the recognition of the Cree in Ouje-Bougoumou as the ninth Cree band, in accordance with the Cree-Naskapi
of Quebec Act. Nowadays, Canada should officially recognize this new Cree band, which was omitted in the hon. member's motion, and put in place a process to establish this new village.
Madam Speaker, the James bay and Northern Quebec Agreement divides the lands in three caterogies: the first category includes lands to be controlled solely by the native people; the second category comprises provincial public lands on which the natives have the exclusive right to hunt, fish and trap; and finally the third category is made up of public lands belonging to the province.
Since the James Bay and northern Quebec Agreement was signed 12 years ago the Governments of Canada and Quebec paid more than $1 billion in cash and services to the 17,000 native people of Northern Quebec living in the ridings of Abitibi and Manicouagan. On-going payments by Canada under the agreements amount to more than $100 million a year.
The Inuit, Cree and Naskapi people have been using these funds to raise the standards of living of their communities. They have shown outstanding ingeniosity and a remarkable spirit of entreprise.
The most enduring benefit of the agreements is that the native people have been able to gain better control over their own future. This very positive climate was highlighted by the July 13, 1984 enactment of the legislation governing Quebec Crees and Naskapis. Crees and Naskapees do now have the power to look after all matters related to their land and affairs. Inuit have also taken charge of their own affairs as a result of the James Bay and northern Quebec convention.
Madam Speaker, we must always remember that in the vast territory of Northern Quebec, in my constituency and that of my colleague of Manicouagan, there are several cities and places that belong to, or rather should I say that are presently inhabited by white people, such as Chapais, Chibougamau, Matagami, Joutel et Lebel-sur-Quevillon. And there is also the buffer zone established by the James Bay convention which exceeds a little bit the James Bay municipality located at the 49th parallel. It represents a vast territory and that is why it is important to consult our people before introducing a bill.
November 23, 1990

Madam Speaker, before tabling a legislation to provide for an additional federal constituency in Northern Quebec, we will have to ask the Inuit, the Cree, the Naskapi and the permanent residents of the North, as well as the Cree-Naskapi Commission under the chairmanship of the hon. Rejean F. Paul, justice of the Superior Court, to present us with a draft legislation to provide for an additional federal constituency. The success of this collective effort will be a model of co-operation between our native friends and the members of the House of Commons.
This is not an easy challenge, but I am confident that our joint efforts will enable us to set up a northern federal constituency in Quebec. Norkurmik Marialuk.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   NORTHERN QUEBEC REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to support the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace on his motion. I do so, not necessarily because I spent five years or so in the constituency of my friend from Abitibi, but mainly because I have spent most of my life in northern communities and I feel that I can speak with some authority on the kind of approach that the hon. member suggests. I must congratulate the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for his approach to this.
To a certain extent, in our democratic structure in Canada and in a large part of the world, we have been seduced by the idea that representation by population, the old "rep by pop" approach, is the proper and most fair way of representation across the country. That motto, "rep by pop", has been the motto of electoral democracy over the years. We should not really knock it because it is still the essence of what we believe in as the democratic base of the country-one vote for one member and representation in the governing body by equal numbers.
Democracy can sometimes be undermined by the majority. We face it every day in the House. The ruling party, which represents a minority of the people in Canada but has a majority of the seats, marches over the will of the people without much concern for what the people of Canada think. It is sort of jack-boot democracy, if you would call it that. But that, Madam Speaker, is another story.
Private Members' Business
Every minority, every group, has the right to have representation in the House. That often does not happen. Theoretically, I suppose, we could expect the House would be a mirror image of the representation of the various groups of people across the country, but that is not likely to happen. It has not happened in the past and it is unlikely to happen in the future.
We can do something to allow certain geographic areas to have the kind of representation which, because of our immense geography in the country, makes it possible and necessary to vary the rule of representation by population. Many live in vast areas of this land and have not been directly represented in the House at any time.
We have solved the problem, as the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace has pointed out, in many places. We solved it in the Northwest Territories. We solved it in the Yukon. We established representation in those areas, regardless of how many people happen to live in those particular areas. We have also made some room for a specific kind of regional representation by varying the numbers of electors that are needed to elect a member in the provinces. For instance, a considerably fewer number of electors are required to elect a member in Prince Edward Island and in Saskatchewan, than are required to elect a member in Ontario or in Quebec. Consequently, to some extent, we have moved away from the idea of representation by population and the number of people required to elect a member to represent them in the House being the same across the country.
But there are large groups and regions that fall through the cracks of our representation. The hon. member has pointed out one or two of these groups by looking at the situation in northern Quebec. I am supporting this particular resolution because the same kind of situation exists in the northern parts of almost every one of our provinces that reaches up to the 54th parallel, or at least to the 60th parallel and above. Quite often, there are very few people in a large area, but those people have a particular point of view.
As I indicated before, I spent a considerable part of my career in those northern areas and have a feeling for the lack of representation they have sometimes felt. A large portion of my time was spent in the Yukon and Northwest Territories where representation is recognized on a regional basis. I have also had some responsibility in

Private Members' Business
northern Saskatchewan where at one time I was the director of education for the northern half of the province.
I suppose it is a good indication of the kind of lack of representation there, in that in the southern half of the province there are something like 85 superintendents of schools. In the northern half, there is only one, but we expect the representation of the large group in the south to be effective in the north.
Northern Saskatchewan, like northern Quebec, has large rural areas, but very little in common with their urban neighbours to the south, or even with their rural neighbours to the south, because a large part of rural Saskatchewan is our farming communities. Consequently, they are being represented by people who do not necessarily feel the same kind of empathy for that group as they would for their more numerous neighbours of the south. I gather that this is the reason for this particular motion and that is to try to give representation to the people who now feel they are not represented as they might be.
The area that we consider to be northern Saskatchewan starts approximately halfway between the U.S. border and the border of the Northwest Territories, just 100 miles or so north of the city of Prince Albert. Therefore, it is approximately half of the territory of the province of Saskatchewan. That territory is presently represented by the hon. member for Prince Albert- Churchill River, who has a great deal of empathy for the people in the north, but recognizes, as he works in that area, that he is not considered by the people to be a northerner.
During the last readjustment of boundaries in northern Saskatchewan, the people of northern Saskatchewan placed before the commission, whose responsibility it was to draw the borders of the constituencies, a number of very broad and responsible briefs which indicated that they felt they would like and needed representation for their particular area separate from that of the more southern areas of the province. The Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act allows a 25 per cent deviation between constituencies within a province. In Saskatchewan the average is about 70,000. The northern part of the province would probably be composed of 35,000 or 40,000, so the deviation would be more than 25 per cent.
That is the reason the commission said it would not continue with the idea of establishing one northern constituency.
I support this particular motion because, if we look at it thoroughly, we will recognize that the idea is proper and that it can be adapted, not only for northern Quebec, but for many other parts of the country where representation is needed and not available at the moment.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   NORTHERN QUEBEC REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:
Narkurmik, Marialuk, Madam Speaker. It is with great interest that I am participating today in the debate on motion M-415, tabled by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. The motion, tabled on April 11, 1989 by my hon. colleague, deals with a situation about which I have been concerned since November of 1988, that is since I was elected as the hon. member for the riding of Manicouagan.
In the next few minutes, I will use both official languages, in order to respect the linguistic duality of the country. I would have liked to be able to address the House in Innutituk, the language of our fellow Inuit who live in the communities of northern Quebec. Unfortunately, I cannot do it. Therefore, I will use the English language, since the Inuit are more familiar with it than with the French.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the riding of Manicouagan, that I have been representing in this house since November of 1988, is one of the largest in the country. It covers an area of over 465,680 square kilometers. It stretches along the north coast of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, from the community of Franquelin to Blanc Sablon, in the eastern reaches of the province of Quebec.

It also stretches from the north coast of the Gulf of St. Lawrence to the northern reaches of both coasts of Ungava Bay. It is a vast and diversified land. The riding territory includes industrialized sections where the major centres of Port-Cartier, Sept-Iles, and Havre-St-Pierre are located. It covers vast areas where logging operations are taking place. It also covers vast areas where there are tourist attractions. The eastern part of the riding, called the Lower North Shore, is made up of 15 fishing villages, most of them linked by sea and air.
November 23, 1990

It also covers vast lands rich in natural resources where the towns of Fermont and Schefferville have been built. Moving further north, the riding of Man-icouagan reaches the southern part of the Bay of Ungava where we find the community of Kuujjuak. The communities on both coasts of the Ungava Bay are also located in the riding of Manicouagan. When we get there, we have an Inuit land.

I recognized from the start of my mandate that it would be difficult for me to give good and frequent services to Inuit communities of Ungava Bay. I planned several times to go and stay there for a while but unfortunately, it was impossible to carry out my wishes.

One must understand that Manicouagan is a large riding with different needs and problems.
Since the fall of 1988, I have tried to be as useful as possible to the people of the northern communities. I have worked actively with my colleague from Abitibi to implement economic programs. I have followed very closely the project of installing an FOL base in Kuujjuak by the Department of National Defence. I felt from the beginning that this project will bring economic activities and employment in Kuujjuak.
While supporting the project, I share the concerns of the community of Kuujjuak and its leaders about the impact that the project could have on the way of life of its people. The Minister of National Defence would be well advised to take the necessary steps to clean up the garbage, debris and drums accumulated in Kuujjuak by the U.S. Air Force during the Second World War and left there. The shore of the Koksoak River and its beaches are littered with drums full of tar. Clean-up procedures satisfactory to the community should be undertaken right away.
After the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform and Party Financing was established, I had several meetings and discussions with its chairman, Mr. Pierre Lortie, on the problems of representations for the northern communities. These discussions led to the visit to Kuujjuak by the royal commission. It gave the Inuit leaders the opportunity to express their view on northern representation and participation in the Canadian democratic process and in the Canadian government.
Private Members' Business
In a letter sent to the commission chairman and to Mr. Jimmy Johannes, Chairman of the Kativik Regional government, I strongly supported the position of the Inuit leaders. In my letter I stated: "I fully support the position of the Inuit people as outlined in your brief." I also said: "The time is long overdue for a better and more active representation of the native people in the House of Commons."
In my letter to Mr. Pierre Lortie, chairman of the royal commission, I wrote: "I would like to take this opportunity to express the view that all efforts should be made to allow the native communities of the northern part of Quebec to be part of a northern federal riding." I further stated: "The creation of a federal riding that would include all communities located on both shores of the Ungava Bay would allow more normal representation in the House of Commons. The process of self-government for the Inuit and other native populations should include representation by a native person in the House of Commons."
Madam Speaker, you will agree that my position is very clear on this matter and I will keep on working to assure better representation for the people living in the north.

Madam Speaker, it is now time to ask the following question: Does the motion introduced by the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace give a good answer to the expectations of northern populations? I don't think so.
The motion specifies that a new federal constituency should match exactly with the territories covered by the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement signed in 1975.
In this geographical context, what will happen to the native population living in the villages located outside the territory covered by the agreement?
Since the terms of the motion refer to the Naskapi people, I think we must evaluate its impacts on the Naskapi and Montagnais groups living in seperate reserves in Schefferville.

The motion implies two main points: First, that the people of northern Quebec, especially the Inuit, Cree and Naskapi citizens of this region are in need of additional representation in this House, and I agree.

November 23, 1990
Private Members' Business
Second, that the Government of Canada may not be exercising its responsibilities to safeguard the economic, social, cultural and environmental rights of all peoples living in this important region of our country.
I would like for a moment to focus on the second point since I have covered the first aspect quite extensively.
The hon. member calls for additional representation, presumably to address a deterioration in conditions faced by native people in northern Quebec. The facts suggest otherwise.
The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement was signed in November of 1975. This was followed by the signing of the Northeastern Quebec Agreement in 1978. Since the conclusion of these two landmark agreements,
18,000	Cree, Inuit and Naskapi living in these regions have received cash and services totalling more than $1 billion from the Government of Canada and the Government of Quebec.
The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement involved an initial compensation of $225 million. The Northeastern Quebec Agreement provides $9 million in compensation and a subsequent agreement involved various types of compensation, relocation and related funding totalling more than $250 million. These figures are significant in their own way.
By themselves, they do not provide the true appreciation of the profound improvement in the quality of life and health standards which the Cree, Naskapi and Inuit have experienced over the past 12 years.
Each village now has its own dispensaries providing first aid care, home visits and community health services. Communities have been divided into independent municipalities. The Cree school board and the Kativik school board are run entirely by elected representatives of the communities.
The James Bay development has actually resulted in considerably reducing the cost of supplies to northern Quebec communities. The existing highway system has made transportation more accessible. Moreover, Cree-owned Air Creebec and Inuit-owned Air Inuit now supply coastal villages from Val d'Or to the Bay of Ungava.
Housing is yet another area where substantial improvements have been achieved. Cree, Naskapi and Inuit families now live in modern homes. Community construction projects are carried out by the Cree, Naskapi and Inuit themselves.
These are impressive accomplishments by any standard of measurement. They offer solid evidence that the aboriginal peoples of northern Quebec have been able to reap significant and lasting benefits from the James Bay development.
Never before have the Cree, Inuit and Naskapi citizens of this region had more control over their own lives, or enjoyed a higher quality of life and health standards, as demonstrated by the considerable population growth in this region in recent years.
The Cree, Naskapi and Inuit citizens of northern Quebec have made some very significant advances over the past decade, both from an economic perspective and in terms of their over-all quality of life.
The Government of Canada is committed to seeing that this progress is not only sustained, but advanced. We will honour our agreements with the aboriginal peoples of this region, as with aboriginal peoples in all regions of Canada.
I would like to suggest in response to the motion by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that Parliament wait for the report of the Lortie royal commission that is taking place at the present time to see its recommendation on this important aspect.
I would also suggest that members' budgets representing those areas, are funded in such a way that will make it possible for us to open up riding offices in those areas, hiring aboriginal peoples so we can provide a daily and a more appropriate service for the people of these communities.
I will conclude by saying that in my capacity as member of Parliament for the riding of Manicouagan, I will continue to represent the Inuit people to the best of my capacity.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   NORTHERN QUEBEC REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to rise today on motion M-415, brought forward by my honourable colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace. He referred to the James Bay agreement, signed in 1975, which sought to provide better representation for the people of that region. According to this
November 23, 1990

agreement and the northeastern Quebec one, which was signed in 1978, these agreements have allowed native people of that region to improve their standard of living and to better control their own development.
Moreover, with the Cree-Naskapi of Quebec Act, the Cree and Naskapi have been the first native people in Canada to achieve some kind of self-government. Bands administer their lands and the natural resources they are controlling. They maintain the native culture, values and traditions and look after community development.
So, the question is this: Why should the federal government create a new electoral district to better represent the native people of that region when there are systems in place that work properly?
Madam Speaker, I admire the interest the member from Notre-Dame-de-Grace shows in the aboriginal people. Nevertheless, it would be wrong to create an additional constituency in Quebec.
Much still remains to be done and many of their grievances are legitimate. That is why the prime minister made public, on September 25, an action plan in order to settle some of the issues concerning aboriginal people of Canada.
That action plan is not made up of vain promises. It is a realistic and concrete plan made which has four objectives: to settle territorial claims; to improve economic and social conditions in reserves; to enhance relations between aboriginal people and governments; to bring the concerns of aboriginal people into contemporary Canadian society.
During the last two months, you noticed for sure that this government takes land claims very seriously. We said that nothing was more important than that and we kept our word.
As early as the beginning of October, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and his Minister of State sought the co-operation of a number of native leaders having experience with the process of specific claims.
That group asked for our support in the setting up of a task force to have discussions with aboriginal communities throughout the country. We agreed, and the task force was struck and is chaired by Manny Jules of British Columbia. It should submit a report at the beginning of
Private Members' Business
December stating its position on a great many subjects concerning specific claims.
We also made progress in other areas. Policy changes were made to allow the negotiation of land claims in British Columbia. We took the necessary steps to ensure that legal obligations contracted over a century ago concerning the transfer of land entitlements to Treaty Indians are respected.
As a matter of fact, the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs announced a few weeks ago that the government was willing to negotiate Treaty land entitlement claims in Saskatchewan. Negotiations will be based on the Treaty Commissioner's report. We have already announced similar measures in Alberta and Manitoba.
The second objective of the government's action plan is to improve living conditions on Indian reserves. As we all know, while major progress was made in recent years, living conditions on native reserves are in many cases still lower than those of the majority of Canadians.
We are ready to co-operate with Indian leaders and provincial governments in order to introduce a number of improvements to basic community programs and services, like running water, sewers, sanitary facilities and so on. The government will soon announce concrete plans designed to make life easier in all native communities.
The third objective is to improve the relations between native people and governments, that is to make it possible for our native fellow citizens to have the same opportunities as other Canadians to contribute to the growth and prosperity of our country. This, Madam Speaker, is definitely not an easy task.
I am convinced that real progress in that field can only flow from redefining the legal relation between government and native people.
The Indian Act, very seldom amended since it was enacted in 1876, maintains native people in a situation of dependence on the state. It belittles both natives and non-natives.
Native leaders on the task force to which I referred a moment ago are expected to make their recommendations on that issue in the near future, so we are looking forward to unveiling the first of a series of amendments to the Indian Act early next year.

November 23, 1990
Private Members' Business
The ultimate objective is to prepare native people to assume their autonomy within the Canadian Constitution. Native people would thus be able to take control over the development of their communities, upgrade their social and educational systems, and acquire the economic infrastructures they need to live the kind of life which reflects their own culture.
Finally, when the Prime Minister announced the creation of the Citizens' Forum on Canada's future on the first of this month, he set in motion an in-depth review of the fundamental place and the role of native people in Canadian society, which happens to be the fourth phase of the federal government's plan of action.
This initiative gives native people an unprecedented opportunity to share their concerns and their hopes with the Canadian public and to insure that their ideas will be considered when we redefine the constitutional status of our country.
Much has passed since our honourable colleague, the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, introduced his motion. The government of Canada has clearly demonstrated, over the last few months, its will to find a resolution to the problems affecting the aboriginal people.
I am convinced, Madam Speaker, that the policy plan implemented by the federal government to deal with the problems of the aboriginal communities will be successful. My colleagues in the House will no doubt agree that a comprehensive program like the one proposed by the government is more appropriate than any initiative pertaining only to a single region or a single part of the country, as regards its representation in this humble assembly.
